A greenish dark blue color; the color of indigo dye.
having a deep purplish-blue colour

intimidate.ety: From Medieval Latin intimidātus, perfect passive participle of Latin intimidō (“to intimidate, terrify”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“in”) + timidus (“afraid, timid”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix); see timid.

en: A complicated irregular network of passages or paths, especially underground or covered, in which it is difficult to find one's way.
A maze formed by paths separated by high hedges.
To enclose in a labyrinth, or as though in a labyrinth.
To arrange in the form of a labyrinth.

labyrinth.ety: From Middle English laberynt, laberynthe, from Latin labyrinthus, from Ancient Greek λᾰβύρῐνθος (lăbúrĭnthos, “a maze”).

ex.ja: 四天王も倒した、クソ長い地下迷宮もクリアした。

note.ja: ギリシャ語 labyrinthos から。クレタ島のミノタウロスの迷宮。「迷宮」。

en: Concealment; the state of being latent; the state of being hidden.
Dormancy; the state of being inactive.

note.ja: latent（潜在的な）+ -cy。ラテン語 latere（隠れている）。「潜伏・遅延」。

en: A speculative place or state, thought possibly to be on the edge of the bottomless pit of Hell, where the souls of innocent deceased peop…

Often followed by under: to pass under something, especially while bending backwards.

limbo.ety:
The noun is derived from Middle English limbo, lymbo (“place where innocent souls exist temporarily until they can enter heaven”), from Latin limbō, the ablative singular of limbus (“border, edge; hem; fringe, tassel”) (notably in expressions like in limbō (“in limbo”) and e limbō (“out of limbo”)); further etymology uncertain, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *lemb- (“to hang limply or loosely”), from Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“to hang down loosely (?)”). Doublet of limp.
The verb is derived from the noun.

note.ja: ラテン語 in limbo（縁に）から。limbus（縁）。天国と地獄の境 →「どっちつかずの状態」。踊りのリンボーは別語。

en: To stay or remain in a place or situation, especially as if unwilling to depart or not easily able to do so.
To remain alive or existent although still proceeding toward death or extinction; to die gradually.

linger.ety: From Middle English lengeren, frequentative of lengen (“to stay, dwell, tarry”), from Old English lenġan (“to lengthen, delay, extend”), from Proto-West Germanic *langijan, from Proto-Germanic *langijaną (compare West Frisian lingje (“to linger”), Dutch lengen, German längen, Icelandic lengja (“to lengthen”)), related to the root of English long. Equivalent to linge or long + -er (frequentative verb suffix).

ex.en: This superstition still lingers on among them.
ex.ja: その迷信は彼らの間で今なお残っている。

ex.en: He lingered in the classroom after school was over.
ex.ja: 彼は授業が終わった後も教室でぶらぶらしていた。

ex.en: The vision that was planted in my senses still silently lingers.
ex.ja: その幻は意識の中に宿り、静寂のなかで動かない。

note.ja: 古英語 lengan（長引かせる）から。long と同系。「ぐずぐず残る」。

en: A collection point for mail intended for onward delivery, a secure box or receptacle for this purpose.
A delivery point for mail, a box, compartment or slot for this purpose.

ex.ja: 「これ、どこにあったの？」「ポストだよ」

en: The protruding part of an animal's head which includes the nose, mouth and jaws.
A device used to prevent an animal from biting or eating, which is worn on its snout.
To bind or confine an animal's mouth by putting a muzzle, as to prevent it from eating or biting.

note.ja: ラテン語 obliviosus（忘れっぽい）から。「気づかない」。oblivion と同じ。

en: Any of many gastropod mollusks, having no (or only a rudimentary) shell.
A bullet or other projectile fired from a firearm; in modern usage, generally refers to a shotgun slug.
To drink quickly; to gulp; to down.
To take part in casual carpooling; to form ad hoc, informal carpools for commuting, essentially a variation of ride-share commuting and h…

ex.ja: ウィスキーの水割りをガッツリ飲んだ。

en: Irritatingly pleased with oneself; offensively self-complacent, self-satisfied.
Showing smugness; showing self-complacency, self-satisfaction.
to adopt an offensively self-complacent expression.

smug.ety:
Originally "spruce, neat," from Low German smuk (“pretty”), from Middle Low German smuk (“lithe, delicate, neat, trim”), although the g of the English word is not easily explained. The ultimate source should be Proto-West Germanic *smeugan (“to crawl, creep”).
From the Low German derived also North Frisian smok, Danish smuk and Swedish smukk (now obsolete or dialectal).
Compare also Middle High German gesmuc (“ornament”) and smücken (“to dress, to adorn”), both ultimately from smiegen (“to press to, insert, wrap, to nestle”), hence German schmiegen, Schmuck and schmücken. The adjective schmuck

ex.ja: 彼のきざな態度は頭にくる。

ex.en: I think that things like animal rights are really just humanity being smug.
ex.ja: 動物愛護とか所詮人間の自己満足だと思う。

note.ja: 低地ドイツ語 smuk（こぎれいな）から。「こぎれいな」→「ひとりよがりの」。

en: The musical part higher in pitch than alto, typically encompassing the range of the treble clef.
A person or instrument that performs the soprano part.
To sing or utter with high pitch.

soprano.ety: Borrowed from Italian soprano, from Vulgar Latin *superānus, adjective from preposition Latin super (“above”). Doublet of sovereign, from the same Latin root via Old French.

ex.en: She is famous as a soprano.
ex.ja: 彼女はソプラノ歌手として有名だ。

ex.en: She is famed as a soprano.
ex.ja: 彼女はソプラノ歌手として有名だ。

ex.en: I was a better alto but was selected as a mezzo-soprano.
ex.ja: わたしはアルトの方が良かったんだけど、メゾソプラノに入れられた。

note.ja: イタリア語 soprano（上の）から。sopra（上に）、ラテン語 supra。「最高音部」。super と同じ。

en: A computer application for organization, analysis, and storage of data in tabular form.
A document created with such an application.
To model or compute by means of a spreadsheet.

ex.en: Once you get the hang of it, spreadsheet software is really useful.
ex.ja: 表計算ソフトは、覚えておくと何かと便利よ。

note.ja: spread（広げる）+ sheet（紙）。広げた大きな帳簿 →「表計算ソフト」。

The hamstring of a quadruped.

tendon.ety: Borrowed from French tendon or Medieval Latin tendō, from Ancient Greek τένων (ténōn, “sinew, tendon”), modified by association with the verb tendō (“to stretch”). Compare Middle English thenoun.

note.ja: ラテン語 tendere（伸ばす）から。筋肉と骨をつないで張るもの →「腱」。

en: Possessing or showing courage or determination; brave, heroic.
Characterized by or done with bravery or valour.

valiant.ety: From Middle English vailaunt (“having or showing courage or valour, valiant; characterized by valour; powerful, strong; person of valour or strength; excellent, worthy; beneficial, useful; valuable; legally valid, binding”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman vaillaunt, vaylant [and other forms], and Old French vailant, vaillant (“brave, valiant; having value, valuable”) [and other forms], from the present participle of valoir (“to have value; to be worth”), from Latin valēre (“to have value; to be worth; to be strong; to have influence or power”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂welh₁

note.ja: 古フランス語 vaillant（強い）から。ラテン語 valere（強い）。「勇敢な」。valor、valid と同じ val。

en: A member of a vigilance committee.
A person who acts outside of legal authority, often violently, to punish or avenge a crime, right a perceived wrong, etc.

vigilante.ety: Borrowed from Spanish vigilante (“watchman, guard”), from Latin vigilans. Doublet of vigilant.

note.ja: スペイン語 vigilante（見張り）から。ラテン語 vigilare（目を覚ましている）。「自警団員」。vigilant と同じ。

en: A venomous snake in the family Viperidae.
Any venomous snake.

viper.ety: From Middle French vipere, from Old French vipre, from Latin vīpera, contracted from vīvipara f (“viviparous”, adj.), from vīvus (“alive”, adj.) + parere (“to bear”, verb). Doublet of weever and wyvern.

note.ja: ラテン語 vipera ＝ vivus（生きた）+ parere（産む）。卵ではなく子を産むと考えられたことから。

en: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday or Friday, but not Saturday or Sunday.
Saturday, Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, but not Friday.

weekday.ety: Inherited from Middle English wykeday, from Old English wicdæġ (“weekday”), from Proto-West Germanic *wikadag, from Proto-Germanic *wikadagaz (“weekday”). By surface analysis, compound of week + day. Compare West Frisian wikedei (“weekday”), Dutch weekdag (“weekday”), German Low German Wekendag (“weekday”), German Wochentag (“weekday”), Danish ugedag (“weekday”), Swedish veckodag (“weekday”), Norwegian ukedag (“weekday”), Faroese vikudagur (“weekday”), Icelandic vikudagur (“weekday”).

ex.en: The weekdays are: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday.
ex.ja: 平日は、月火水木金です。

ex.en: She is always busy on weekdays.
ex.ja: 彼女の平日はいつも忙しい。

ex.en: Weekdays Monday through Friday, from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.
ex.ja: 月曜日から金曜日の平日の間、午前9時から午後5時までです。

note.ja: week（週）+ day（日）。「平日」。

en: A small furrow, ridge or crease in an otherwise smooth surface.
A line or crease in the skin, especially when caused by age or fatigue.
To make wrinkles in; to cause to have wrinkles.
To pucker or become uneven or irregular.

wrinkle.ety: From Middle English wrinkle, wrynkel (“crease, fold, wrinkle”), from the verb (see below). Cognate with Dutch wrinkel (“wrinkle, crease”). Compare also Middle English runkel (“wrinkle”), from Old Norse hrukka (“wrinkle”), from Proto-Germanic *hrunkwǭ (“wrinkle, crease”), whence also French fronce (“crooked smile, scowl, frown”), German Runzel (“wrinkle”), Danish rynke (“wrinkle”), Swedish rynka and rynkla (“wrinkle”).

ex.en: His blue coat was dirty and wrinkled.
ex.ja: 彼の青いコートは汚れていてしわくちゃだった。

ex.en: She has started to get a few wrinkles around her eyes.
ex.ja: 彼女の目の回りには、小じわができてきた。

ex.en: I ironed out the wrinkles in my pants.
ex.ja: 私はズボンのしわをアイロンで伸ばした。

note.ja: 古英語 gewrinclod（ねじれた）から。wrench と同系。「しわ」。

en: The act of abstracting, separating, withdrawing, or taking away; withdrawal; the state of being taken away.
The taking surreptitiously for one's own use part of the property of another; purloining.

abstraction.ety: From Middle English abstraccyone; either from Middle French abstraction or from Medieval Latin abstrāctiō (“separation”), from Latin abstrahō (“draw away”). Equivalent to abstract + -ion.

note.ja: abs（離れて）+ tract（引く）+ ion。具体物から引き離すこと →「抽象（化）・放心状態」。

en: To move upward, to fly, to soar.
To slope in an upward direction.

ascend.ety: From Middle English ascenden, borrowed from Old French ascendre, from Latin ascendō (“to go up, climb up to”), from ad (“to”) + scandō (“to climb”); see scan. Unrelated to accede other than common ad prefix.

ex.en: This mountain path ascends to the beautiful lake.
ex.ja: この山道を登ると美しい湖に出る。

ex.en: The road ascends to the village.
ex.ja: 道は上り坂になってその村に出る。

ex.en: The smoke ascended into the air.
ex.ja: 煙は空中へと舞い上がった。

note.ja: a（〜へ）+ scend（登る）。上へ登る →「上る・昇進する」。descend（下る）と対。

en: Paying attention; noticing, watching, listening, or attending closely.
Courteous; mindful.

attentive.ety: From Middle English attentif, attentijf, from Old French attentif.

ex.en: They were most attentive to his speech.
ex.ja: みんなは彼の話を注意深く聞いた。

ex.en: Mary is very attentive, isn't she?
ex.ja: メアリーはとても気が利くよね。

ex.en: She is very attentive to her grandmother.
ex.ja: 彼女はおばあちゃんをたいそう大事にする。

note.ja: at（〜へ）+ tent（伸ばす）+ ive。心を〜へ向けている →「注意深い・気配りのある」。

en: A field, stadium or park where ball, especially baseball, is played.
The general vicinity; somewhere close; a broad approximation.
Approximate; close; on the right order of magnitude.
To make a rough estimate of.

ballpark.ety: From ball + park. Sense 2 related to ballpark figure.

ex.en: He showed me the way to the ballpark.
ex.ja: 彼は私に球場への道を教えてくれた。

ex.en: You can go to the ballpark on this bus.
ex.ja: このバスに乗れば球場へ行けます。

ex.en: Could you tell me how to get to the ballpark?
ex.ja: 野球場にどうやって行ったらよいか教えていただけませんか。

note.ja: ball（球）+ park（場所）。「野球場」→ 球場の範囲内 →「概算（ballpark figure）」。

A similar pointed structure forming the nose and mouth of various animals, such as turtles, platypuses, whales, etc.
To strike with the beak.
To seize with the beak.

ex.en: Woodpeckers peck tree trunks with their long pointed beaks and eat insects found there.
ex.ja: きつつきは、長く尖ったくちばしで、木の幹をつついて、中にいる虫を食べます。

note.ja: 古フランス語 bec（くちばし）から。ケルト語に由来する。

en: A colour, variously defined from a pale brown, to a yellow greyish off-white.
Debeige; a kind of woollen or mixed dress goods.
Having a slightly yellowish gray colour, as that of unbleached wool.
Comfortably dull and unadventurous, in a way that suggests middle-class suburbia.

beige.ety: Unadapted borrowing from French (dialectal) beige, from Old French bege (“color of undyed wool or cotton”), from an Alpine language (compare Franco-Provençal bézho, Romansch besch (“dull grey”)), from Vulgar Latin *bysseus (“cottony grey”) (compare French bis, Catalan bis, Italian bigio), from Late Latin byssus (“cotton”), from Ancient Greek βύσσος (bússos, “cotton homespun”), from Semitic (compare Hebrew/Aramaic בוץ (būṣ)). Doublet of bice.

ex.en: She stained the wall beige.
ex.ja: 彼女は壁をベージュ色にした。

note.ja: フランス語 beige（未染色の羊毛の色）から。

en: An act of irreverence or contempt toward a god or toward something considered sacred; an impious act, utterance, view, etc.
An act of irreverence towards anything considered inviolable; the act of disregarding a convention.

blasphemy.ety: From Middle English blasfemie, from Old French blasfemie, from Ecclesiastical Latin blasphēmia, from Ancient Greek βλασφημία (blasphēmía, “profanity”), from βλασφημέω (blasphēméō, “to slander”). Displaced native Old English tāl.

ex.en: "Novels? I hate novels." Oh muse, forgive her blasphemy.
ex.ja: 「小説？　あたし小説は嫌ひですの」 　おゝ、ミュウズよ、彼女の冒涜を赦せ。

note.ja: ギリシャ語 blasphēmia（冒涜）から。blaptein（害する）+ phēmē（言葉）。「神をののしる言葉」。blame と同じ語源。

ex.ja: ブルーベリーをとった後、タルトを作る。

A male pig.

To clean (metal) using a branner.

note.ja: 古フランス語 bren（ぬか）から。「ぬか・ふすま」。

A field officer of the highest grade, below general officers, NATO grade OF-7.

Unwieldy.

bulky.ety: From Middle English bulki, boulky, equivalent to bulk + -y.

ex.en: This box is too bulky to carry.
ex.ja: この箱はかさばりすぎて運べない。

ex.en: This is bulky, so I'll send it by home delivery.
ex.ja: これはかさばるから宅配便で送ろう。

ex.en: These presents are really bulky.
ex.ja: このお土産かさばるなぁ。

note.ja: bulk（かさ）+ -y。「かさばる」。

ex.ja: トムはカメラマンだよ。

ex.ja: 彼は大学卒業後カメラマンになった。

en: Death and destruction.
The corpses, gore, etc. that remain after a massacre.

carnage.ety: Borrowed from Middle French carnage, from a Norman or Picard variant Old Northern French) of Old French charnage, from char (“flesh”), or from Vulgar Latin *carnaticum (“slaughter of animals”), itself from Latin carnem, accusative of caro (“flesh”). en: To congratulate or reward.
To praise or acclaim.

commend.ety: From Middle English commenden, from Old French comender, from Latin commendō (“commend, entrust to, commit, recommend”), from com- + mandō (“to commit, intrust, enjoin”), from manus (“hand”) + dō (“to put”). Doublet of command.

ex.en: We commended him for his good work.
ex.ja: 立派な仕事をしたと彼を誉めた。

en: Pertaining to a conclusion.
Providing an end to something; decisive.

conclusive.ety: From French conclusif, from Late Latin conclusivus, from Latin conclūsīvē (“conclusively”), from past participle of concludere.

note.ja: con（完全に）+ clus（閉じる）+ ive。完全に閉じる →「決定的な・確実な」。

en: Having the quality of preserving from loss, decay, or injury.
A school or clinic for orphans.
A music school.

conservatory.ety: From Medieval Latin cōnservātōrius directly and via French conservatoire, from cōnservāre (“to conserve, to preserve”) + -torius (“-atory: forming related adjectives”) and/or conservator (“conservator, preserver, protector”) + -ius (“-y: forming related adjectives”).

note.ja: con（完全に）+ serv（保つ）+ atory。（植物を）保護する所 →「温室」、（音楽を）保存し伝える所 →「音楽学校」。

en: Consciously thoughtful and observant (often of other people and their rights, needs, feelings and comfort).
Characterised by careful and conscious thought.

ex.en: You should be more considerate of your parents.
ex.ja: 君は両親に対してもっと思いやりの心を持つべきです。

en: A sudden or unexpected failure.
A ludicrous or humiliating situation. Some effort that went quite wrong.

fiasco.ety:
Borrowed from Italian fiasco (“bottle, flask”), from Late Latin flasca, flascō (“bottle, container”), from Frankish *flaskā (“bottle, flask”) from Proto-Germanic *flaskǭ (“bottle”); see flask.
“Failure” sense comes through French faire fiasco from Italian theatrical slang far fiasco (literally “to make a bottle”), of uncertain origin; perhaps from an expression fare il fiasco, meaning to play a game with the forfeit that the loser will buy the next bottle or round of drinks.
Doublet of flacon, flagon, and flask.

ex.en: We'll never live this fiasco down.
ex.ja: この失敗、きっと一生、言われつづけるなあ。

note.ja: イタリア語 fiasco（瓶）から。far fiasco（瓶を作る）がガラス職人の失敗を指したことからとされる。「大失敗」。flask と同じ。

The person or thing in the fifteenth position.
One of fifteen equal parts of a whole.

fifteenth.ety: Inherited from Middle English fiftenthe, fiftethe, from Old English fīftēoþa, equivalent to fifteen + -th.

ex.en: Who is the fifteenth?

en: A state of terror excited by the sudden appearance of danger; sudden and violent fear, usually of short duration; a sudden alarm.
Someone strange, ugly or shocking, producing a feeling of alarm or aversion.

fright.ety:
From Middle English fright, furht, from Old English fryhtu, fyrhto (“fright, fear, dread, trembling, horrible sight”), from Proto-Germanic *furhtį̄ (“fear”), from Proto-Indo-European *pr̥k- (“to fear”).
Cognate with Scots fricht (“fright”), Old Frisian fruchte (“fright”), Low German frucht (“fright”), Middle Dutch vrucht, German Furcht (“fear, fright”), Danish frygt (“fear”), Swedish fruktan (“fear, fright, dread”), Gothic 𐍆𐌰𐌿𐍂𐌷𐍄𐌴𐌹 (faurhtei, “fear, horror, fright”). Compare possibly Albanian frikë (“fear, fright, dread, danger”).

ex.ja: 大きな物音で私は肝をつぶした。

ex.en: Fright gave the old lady heart failure.
ex.ja: 突然の恐怖に老婆は心臓麻痺を起こした。

ex.en: Aside from fright she was not injured.
ex.ja: 彼女は脅えただけで怪我はなかった。

note.ja: 古英語 fyrhto（恐怖）から。「恐怖」。frighten と同じ。

en: Impudence or brazenness; temerity; chutzpah.

To chafe, to rub or subject to friction; to create a sore on the skin.
To bother or trouble.

gall.ety:
From Middle English galle, from Old English ġealla, galla, from Proto-West Germanic *gallā, from Proto-Germanic *gallǭ.
The figurative senses (e.g., impudence, brazenness, chutzpah) are related to the literal sense (i.e., bile) via the lasting linguocultural effects of humorism, which governed Western medicine for many centuries before the advent of scientific medicine.
Related to Dutch gal, German Galle, Swedish galle, galla, Ancient Greek χολή (kholḗ). Also remotely related with yellow and gold.

ex.en: For gall bladder surgery, go down this hall and take a right.
ex.ja: 胆のうの手術でしたら、この廊下をずっと行って右に曲がってください。

ex.en: His sarcasm galls me.
ex.ja: 彼の当てこすりはかんにさわる。

jog.ety:
Of uncertain origin. Originally with the meaning of "to shake up and down." Possibly from Middle English joggen, a variant of jaggen (“to pierce, prod, stir up, arouse”); see jag (“sharp projection”).
Or, perhaps an early alteration of English shog (“to jolt, shake; depart, go”), from Middle English shoggen, schoggen (“to shake up and down, jog”), from Middle Dutch schocken (“to jolt, bounce”) or Middle Low German schoggen, schocken (“to shog”), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *skukkōn (“to move, shake, tremble”), possibly related to *skakan (“to shake, stir”). More at shock.
